---
title: "Unsupervised Learning"
---

Unsupervised learning searches for structure without an observed
response. This lecture focuses on clustering, dimension reduction for
exploration, and the risks of over-interpreting discovered patterns.

## Learning Objectives

- Distinguish supervised prediction from unsupervised structure
  discovery.
- Apply PCA for visualization and compression.
- Compare k-means and hierarchical clustering.
- Evaluate unsupervised results with stability, context, and
  downstream usefulness.

## Core Ideas

Without a response variable, there is no single test error to optimize.
The quality of an unsupervised analysis depends on the distance metric,
preprocessing, stability, and whether the discovered structure answers
a meaningful question.

## Clustering

K-means clustering partitions observations into $K$ groups by minimizing
within-cluster squared distance:

$$
\sum_{k=1}^{K} \sum_{i \in C_k} \|x_i - \bar x_k\|^2.
$$

The analyst chooses $K$, so clustering should be checked for stability
and interpretability.

```r
set.seed(571)
x <- scale(USArrests)
km <- kmeans(x, centers = 3, nstart = 20)
km$cluster
```

Hierarchical clustering builds a tree of nested clusters. It requires a
distance metric and linkage rule.

```r
hc <- hclust(dist(x), method = "complete")
plot(hc)
rect.hclust(hc, k = 3)
```

## PCA for Unsupervised Structure

PCA is often used before clustering to visualize high-dimensional data.
It can reveal dominant directions of variation, but those directions are
not automatically the most meaningful scientific dimensions.

## Cluster Analysis Example

Use a data set with several numeric features. Scale the data, visualize
PCA scores, run k-means for multiple values of $k$, and compare with a
hierarchical clustering solution.

## Stability Practice

Practice by clustering a scaled numeric data set, comparing several
values of $K$, and explaining whether the clusters are stable and
meaningful.
